entries.d09b4add27a2d043cdb95695fbf7d9c0d6faefc0: <div sID="gen12121" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="91" osisID="Ps.91" sID="Ps.91"/> <div eID="gen12121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12122" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12123" type="x-p"/> Some of the ancients were of opinion that Moses was the penman, not only of the foregoing psalm, which is expressly said to be his, but also of the eight that next follow it; but that cannot be, for <reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11">Ps. xcv.</reference> is expressly said to be penned by David, and long after Moses, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.7">Heb. iv. 7</reference>. It is probable that this psalm also was penned by David; it is a writ of protection for all true believers, not in the name of king David, or under his broad seal; he needed it himself, especially if the psalm was penned, as some conjecture it was, at the time of the pestilence which was sent for his numbering the people; but in the name of the King of kings, and under the broad seal of Heaven. Observe, I. The psalmist's own resolution to take God for his keeper (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">ver. 2</reference>), from which he gives both direction and encouragement to others, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">ver. 9</reference>. II. The promises which are here made, in God's name, to all those that do so in sincerity. 1. They shall be taken under the peculiar care of Heaven, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">4</reference>. 2. They shall be delivered from the malice of the powers of darkness (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.5">5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">6</reference>), and that by a distinguishing preservation, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.7-Ps.91.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. 3. They shall be the charge of the holy angels, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.10-Ps.91.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. 4. They shall triumph over their enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.13">ver. 13</reference>. 5. They shall be the special favourites of God himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.14-Ps.91.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. In singing this we must shelter ourselves under, and then solace ourselves in, the divine protection. Many think that to Christ, as Mediator, these promises do primarily belong (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>), not because to him the devil applied one of these promises (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">Matt. iv. 6</reference>), but because to him they are very applicable, and, coming through him, they are more sweet and sure to all believers.
entries.e911966666601252bb2e1150387260429eda3e95: <div eID="gen12123" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12122" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of Believers.</title> <div sID="gen12124" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. <hi type="super">2</hi> I will say of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">He is</hi> my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust. <hi type="super">3</hi> Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, <hi type="italic">and</hi> from the noisome pestilence. <hi type="super">4</hi> He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth <hi type="italic">shall be thy</hi> shield and buckler. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; <hi type="italic">nor</hi> for the arrow <hi type="italic">that</hi> flieth by day; <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Nor</hi> for the pestilence <hi type="italic">that</hi> walketh in darkness; <hi type="italic">nor</hi> for the destruction <hi type="italic">that</hi> wasteth at noonday. <hi type="super">7</hi> A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; <hi type="italic">but</hi> it shall not come nigh thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked. <div eID="gen12124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12125" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen12125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12126" type="x-p"/> I. A great truth laid down in general, That all those who live a life of communion with God are constantly safe under his protection, and may therefore preserve a holy serenity and security of mind at all times (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that dwells,</hi> that sits down, <hi type="italic">in the secret place of the Most High, shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty;</hi> he that by faith chooses God for his guardian shall find all that in him which he needs or can desire. Note, 1. It is the character of a true believer that he <hi type="italic">dwells in the secret place of the Most High;</hi> he is at home in God, returns to God, and reposes in him as his rest; he acquaints himself with inward religion, and makes heart-work of the service of God, worships within the veil, and loves to be alone with God, to converse with him in solitude. 2. It is the privilege and comfort of those that do so that they <hi type="italic">abide under the shadow of the Almighty;</hi> he shelters them, and comes between them and every thing that would annoy them, whether storm or sunshine. They shall not only have an admittance, but a residence, under God's protection; he will be their rest and refuge for ever. <div eID="gen12126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12127" type="x-p"/> II. The psalmist's comfortable application of this to himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will say of the Lord,</hi> whatever others say of him, "<hi type="italic">He is my refuge;</hi> I choose him as such, and confide in him. Others make idols their refuge, but I will say of Jehovah, the true and living God, He is <hi type="italic">my refuge:</hi> any other is a <hi type="italic">refuge of lies.</hi> He is a refuge that will not fail me; for he is <hi type="italic">my fortress and strong-hold.</hi>" Idolaters called their idols <hi type="italic">Mahuzzim,</hi> their <hi type="italic">most strong-hold</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.39">Dan. xi. 39</reference>), but therein they deceived themselves; those only secure themselves that make the Lord their God, their fortress. There being no reason to question his sufficiency, fitly does it follow, <hi type="italic">In him will I trust.</hi> If Jehovah be our God, our refuge, and our fortress, what can we desire which we may not be sure to find in him? He is neither fickle nor false, neither weak nor mortal; he is God and not man, and therefore there is no danger of being disappointed in him. <hi type="italic">We know whom we have trusted.</hi> <div eID="gen12127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12128" type="x-p"/> III. The great encouragement he gives to others to do likewise, not only from his own experience of the comfort of it (for in that there might possibly be a fallacy), but from the truth of God's promise, in which there neither is nor can be any deceit (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.3-Ps.91.4">v. 3, 4</reference>, &c.): <hi type="italic">Surely he shall deliver thee.</hi> Those who have themselves found the comfort of making God their refuge cannot but desire that others may do so. Now here it is promised, <div eID="gen12128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12129" type="x-p"/> 1. That believers shall be kept from those mischiefs which they are in imminent danger of, and which would be fatal to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">from the snare of the fowler,</hi> which is laid unseen and catches the unwary prey on a sudden, and <hi type="italic">from the noisome pestilence,</hi> which seizes men unawares and against which there is no guard. This promise protects, (1.) The natural life, and is often fulfilled in our preservation from those dangers which are very threatening and very near, while yet we ourselves are not apprehensive of them, any more than the bird is of <hi type="italic">the snare of the fowler.</hi> We owe it, more than we are sensible, to the care of the divine Providence that we have been kept from infectious diseases and out of the hands of the wicked and unreasonable. (2.) The spiritual life, which is protected by divine grace from the temptations of Satan, which are as the <hi type="italic">snares of the fowler,</hi> and from the contagion of sin, which is the <hi type="italic">noisome pestilence.</hi> He that has given grace to be the glory of the soul will create a defence upon all that glory. <div eID="gen12129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12130" type="x-p"/> 2. That God himself will be their protector; those must needs be safe who have him for their keeper, and successful for whom he undertakes (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall cover thee,</hi> shall keep thee <hi type="italic">secret</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Ps. xxxi. 20</reference>), and so keep thee safe, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 5</reference>. God protects believers, (1.) With the greatest tenderness and affection, which is intimated in that, <hi type="italic">He shall cover thee with his feathers, under his wings,</hi> which alludes to the hen <hi type="italic">gathering her chickens under wings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>. By natural instinct she not only protects them, but calls them under that protection when she sees them in danger, not only keeps them safe, but cherishes them and keeps them warm. To this the great God is pleased to compare his care of his people, who are helpless as the chickens, and easily made a prey of, but are invited to trust under the shadow of the wings of the divine promise and providence, which is the periphrasis of a proselyte to the true religion, that he has come to <hi type="italic">trust under the wings of the God of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">Ruth ii. 12</reference>. (2.) With the greatest power and efficacy. Wings and feathers, though spread with the greatest tenderness, are yet weak, and easily broken through, and therefore it is added, <hi type="italic">His truth shall be thy shield and buckler,</hi> a strong defence. God is willing to guard his people as the hen is to guard the chickens, and as able as a man of war in armour. <div eID="gen12130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12131" type="x-p"/> 3. That he will not only keep them from evil, but from the fear of evil, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.5-Ps.91.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Here is, (1.) Great danger supposed; the mention of it is enough to frighten us; night and day we lie exposed, and those that are apt to be timorous will in neither period think themselves safe. When we are retired into our chambers, our beds, and have made all as safe as we can about us, yet there is terror by night, from thieves and robbers, winds and storms, besides those things that are the creatures of fancy and imagination, which are often most frightful of all. We read of <hi type="italic">fear in the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.8">Cant. iii. 8</reference>. There is also a <hi type="italic">pestilence that walketh in darkness,</hi> as that was which slew the first-born of the Egyptians, and the army of the Assyrians. No locks nor bars can shut out diseases, while we carry about with us in our bodies the seeds of them. But surely in the day-time, when we can look about us, we are not so much in danger; yes, there is an <hi type="italic">arrow that flieth by day</hi> too, and yet flies unseen; there is a destruction that wasteth at high-noon, when we are awake and have all our friends about us; even then we cannot secure ourselves, nor can they secure us. It was in the day-time that that pestilence wasted which was sent to chastise David for numbering the people, on occasion of which some think this psalm was penned. But, (2.) Here is great security promised to believers in the midst of this danger: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not be afraid.</hi> God by his grace will keep thee from disquieting distrustful fear (that fear which hath torment) in the midst of the greatest dangers. Wisdom shall keep thee from being causelessly afraid, and faith shall keep thee from being inordinately afraid. Thou shalt not be afraid of the arrow, as knowing that though it may hit thee it cannot hurt thee; if it take away the natural life, yet it shall be so far from doing any prejudice to the spiritual life that it shall be its perfection." A believer <hi type="italic">needs not</hi> fear, and therefore <hi type="italic">should not</hi> fear, any arrow, because the point is off, the poison is out. <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> It is also under divine direction, and will hit where God appoints and not otherwise. Every bullet has its commission. Whatever is done our heavenly Father's will is done; and we have no reason to be afraid of that. <div eID="gen12131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12132" type="x-p"/> 4. That they shall be preserved in common calamities, in a distinguishing way (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.7">v. 7</reference>): "When death rides in triumph, and diseases rage, so that <hi type="italic">thousands and ten thousands</hi> fall, fall by sickness, or fall by the sword in battle, <hi type="italic">fall at thy side, at thy right hand,</hi> and the sight of their fall is enough to frighten thee, and if they fall by the pestilence their falling so near thee may be likely to infect thee, <hi type="italic">yet it shall not come nigh thee,</hi> the death shall not, the fear of death shall not." Those that preserve their purity in times of general corruption may trust God with their safety in times of general desolation. When multitudes die round about us, though thereby we must be awakened to prepare for our own death, yet we must not be <hi type="italic">afraid with any amazement,</hi> nor make ourselves subject to bondage, as many do all their life-time, <hi type="italic">through fear of death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.15">Heb. ii. 15</reference>. The sprinkling of blood secured the first-born of Israel when thousands fell. Nay, it is promised to God's people that they shall have the satisfaction of seeing, not only God's promises fulfilled to them, but his threatenings fulfilled upon those that hate them (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Only with thy eyes shalt thou behold and see the just reward of the wicked,</hi> which perhaps refers to the destruction of the first-born of Egypt by the pestilence, which was both the punishment of the oppressors and the enlargement of the oppressed; this Israel saw when they saw themselves unhurt, untouched. As it will aggravate the damnation of sinners that with their eyes they shall behold and see the reward of the righteous (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.28">Luke xiii. 28</reference>), so it will magnify the salvation of the saints that with their eyes they shall behold and see the destruction of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Isa. lxvi. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Ps. lviii. 10</reference>.
entries.0bec569362865235d4dfd0d083cd43724e36edfa: <div eID="gen12132" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of Believers.</title> <div sID="gen12133" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Because thou hast made the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">which is</hi> my refuge, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the most High, thy habitation; <hi type="super">10</hi> There shall no evil befal thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling. <hi type="super">11</hi> For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. <hi type="super">12</hi> They shall bear thee up in <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet. <hi type="super">14</hi> Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name. <hi type="super">15</hi> He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I <hi type="italic">will be</hi> with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him. <hi type="super">16</hi> With long life will I satisfy him, and show him my salvation. <div eID="gen12133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12134" type="x-p"/> Here are more promises to the same purport with those in the <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1-Ps.91.8">foregoing verses</reference>, and they are exceedingly great and precious, and sure to all the seed. <div eID="gen12134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12135" type="x-p"/> I. The psalmist assures believers of divine protection, from his own experience; and that which he says is the word of God, and what we may rely upon. Observe, 1. The character of those who shall have the benefit and comfort of these promises; it is much the same with that, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">v. 1</reference>. They are such as make <hi type="italic">the Most High their habitation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">v. 9</reference>), as are continually with God and rest in him, as make his name both their temple and their strong tower, as dwell in love and so dwell in God. It is our duty to be at home in God, to make our choice of him, and then to live our life in him as our habitation, to converse with him, and delight in him, and depend upon him; and then it shall be our privilege to be at home in God; we shall be welcome to him as a man to his own habitation, without any let, hindrance, or molestation, from the arrests of the law or the clamours of conscience; then too we shall be safe in him, shall be kept in <hi type="italic">perfect peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa. xxvi. 3</reference>. To encourage us to make the Lord our habitation, and to hope for safety and satisfaction in him, the psalmist intimates the comfort he had had in doing so: "He whom thou makest thy <hi type="italic">habitation is my refuge;</hi> and I have found him firm and faithful, and in him there is room enough, and shelter enough, both for thee and me." <hi type="italic">In my father's house</hi> there <hi type="italic">are many mansions,</hi> one needs not crowd another, much less crowd out another. 2. The promises that are sure to all those who have thus made <hi type="italic">the Most High</hi> their <hi type="italic">habitation.</hi> (1.) That, whatever happens to them, nothing shall hurt them (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">There shall no evil befal thee;</hi> though trouble or affliction befal thee, yet there shall be no real evil in it, for it shall come from the love of God and shall be sanctified; it shall come, not for thy hurt, but for thy good; and though, for <hi type="italic">the present, it be not joyous but grievous,</hi> yet, in the end, it shall yield so well that thou thyself shalt own <hi type="italic">no evil befel thee.</hi> It is not an evil, an only evil, but there is a mixture of good in it and a product of good by it. Nay, not thy person only, but thy dwelling, shall be taken under the divine protection: <hi type="italic">There shall no plague come nigh</hi> that, nothing to do thee or thine any damage." <hi type="italic">Nihil accidere bono viro mali potest—No evil can befal a good man.</hi> Seneca <hi type="italic">De Providentia.</hi> (2.) That the angels of light shall be serviceable to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.11-Ps.91.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. This is a precious promise, and speaks a great deal both of honour and comfort to the saints, nor is it ever the worse for being quoted and abused by the devil in tempting Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">Matt. iv. 6</reference>. Observe, [1.] The charge given to the angels concerning the saints. He who is the Lord of the angels, who gave them their being and gives laws to them, whose they are and whom they were made to serve, <hi type="italic">he shall give his angels a charge over thee,</hi> not only over the church in general, but over every particular believer. The angels <hi type="italic">keep the charge of the Lord their God;</hi> and this is the charge they receive from him. It denotes the great care God takes of the saints, in that the angels themselves shall be charged with them, and employed for them. The charge is <hi type="italic">to keep thee in all thy ways;</hi> here is a limitation of the promise: They <hi type="italic">shall keep thee in thy ways,</hi> that is, "as long as thou keepest in the way of thy duty;" those that go out of that way put themselves out of God's protection. This word the devil left out when he quoted the promise to enforce a temptation, knowing how much it made against him. But observe the extent of the promise; it is <hi type="italic">to keep thee in all thy ways:</hi> even where there is no apparent danger yet we need it, and where there is the most imminent danger we shall have it. Wherever the saints go the angels are charged with them, as the servants are with the children. [2.] The care which the angels take of the saints, pursuant to this charge: <hi type="italic">They shall bear thee up in their hands,</hi> which denotes both their great ability and their great affection. They are able to bear up the saints out of the reach of danger, and they do it with all the tenderness and affection wherewith the nurse carries the little child about in her arms; it speaks us helpless and them helpful. They are condescending in their ministrations; they keep the feet of the saints, lest they <hi type="italic">dash them against a stone,</hi> lest they stumble and fall into sin and into trouble. [3.] That the powers of darkness shall be triumphed over by them (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder.</hi> The devil is called <hi type="italic">a roaring lion, the old serpent, the red dragon;</hi> so that to this promise the apostle seems to refer in that (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">Rom. xvi. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The God of peace shall tread Satan under your feet.</hi> Christ has broken the serpent's head, spoiled our spiritual enemies (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>), and through him <hi type="italic">we are more than conquerors;</hi> for Christ calls us, as Joshua called the captains of Israel, to come and set our feet on the necks of vanquished enemies. Some think that this promise had its full accomplishment in Christ, and the miraculous power which he had over the whole creation, healing the sick, casting out devils, and particularly putting it into his disciples' commission that they should <hi type="italic">take up serpents,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.16.18">Mark xvi. 18</reference>. It may be applied to that care of the divine Providence by which we are preserved from ravenous noxious creatures (<hi type="italic">the wild beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job v. 23</reference>); nay, and have ways and means of taming them, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.7">Jam. iii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen12135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12136" type="x-p"/> II. He brings in God himself speaking words of comfort to the saints, and declaring the mercy he had in store for them, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.14-Ps.91.16">v. 14-16</reference>. Some make this to be spoken to the angels as the reason of the charge given them concerning the saints, as if he had said, "Take care of them, for they are dear to me, and I have a tender concern for them." And now, as before, we must observe, <div eID="gen12136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12137" type="x-p"/> 1. To whom these promises do belong; they are described by three characters:—(1.) They are such as know God's name. His nature we cannot fully know; but by his name he has made himself known, and with that we must acquaint ourselves. (2.) They are such as have set their love upon him; and those who rightly know him will love him, will place their love upon him as the only adequate object of it, will let out their love towards him with pleasure and enlargement, and will fix their love upon him with a resolution never to remove it to any rival. (3.) They are such as call upon him, as by prayer keep up a constant correspondence with him, and in every difficult case refer themselves to him. <div eID="gen12137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12138" type="x-p"/> 2. What the promises are which God makes to the saints. (1.) That he will, in due time, deliver them out of trouble: <hi type="italic">I will deliver him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.14">v. 14</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ps.91.15">v. 15</reference>), denoting a double deliverance, living and dying, a deliverance in trouble and a deliverance out of trouble. If God proportions the degree and continuance of our troubles to our strength, if he keeps us from offending him in our troubles, and makes our death our discharge, at length, from all our troubles, then this promise is fulfilled. See <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Ps. xxxiv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">2 Tim. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">iv. 18</reference>. (2.) That he will, in the mean time, <hi type="italic">be with them in trouble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.91.15">v. 15</reference>. If he does not immediately put a period to their afflictions, yet they shall have his gracious presence with them in their troubles; he will take notice of their sorrows, and <hi type="italic">know their souls in adversity,</hi> will visit them graciously by his word and Spirit, and converse with them, will take their part, will support and comfort them, and sanctify their afflictions to them, which will be the surest token of his presence with them in their troubles. (3.) That herein he will answer their prayers: <hi type="italic">He shall call upon me;</hi> I will pour upon him the spirit of prayer, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">I will answer,</hi> answer by promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Ps. lxxxv. 8</reference>), answer by providences, bringing in seasonable relief, and answer by graces, <hi type="italic">strengthening them with strength in their souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Ps. cxxxviii. 3</reference>); thus he answered Paul with <hi type="italic">grace sufficient,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2 Cor. xii. 9</reference>. (4.) That he will exalt and dignify them: <hi type="italic">I will set him on high,</hi> out of the reach of trouble, above the stormy region, on a rock <hi type="italic">above the waves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Isa. xxxiii. 16</reference>. They shall be enabled, by the grace of God, to look down upon the things of this world with a holy contempt and indifference, to look up to the things of the other world with a holy ambition and concern; and then they are set on high. <hi type="italic">I will honour him;</hi> those are truly honourable whom God puts honour upon by taking them into covenant and communion with himself and designing them for his kingdom and glory, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>. (5.) That they shall have a sufficiency of life in this world (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">With length of days will I satisfy him;</hi> that is, [1.] They shall live long enough: they shall be continued in this world till they have done the work they were sent into this world for and are ready for heaven, and that is long enough. Who would wish to live a day longer than God has some work to do, either by him or upon him? [2.] They shall think it long enough; for God by his grace shall wean them from the world and make them willing to leave it. A man may die young, and yet die full of days, <hi type="italic">satur dierum—satisfied with living.</hi> A wicked worldly man is not satisfied, no, not with long life; he still cries, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> But he that has his treasure and heart in another world has soon enough of this; he would not live always. (6.) That they shall have an eternal life in the other world. This crowns the blessedness: <hi type="italic">I will show him my salvation,</hi> show him <hi type="italic">the Messiah</hi> (so some); good old Simeon was then satisfied with long life when he could say, <hi type="italic">My eyes have seen thy salvation,</hi> nor was there any greater joy to the Old-Testament saints than to see Christ's day, though at a distance. It is more probably that the word refers to the better country, that is, the heavenly, which the patriarchs desired and sought: he <hi type="italic">will show him</hi> that, bring him to that blessed state, the felicity of which consists so much in seeing that face to face which we here see through a glass darkly; and, in the mean time, he will give him a prospect of it. All these promises, some think, point primarily at Christ, and had their accomplishment in his resurrection and exaltation.  <chapter eID="Ps.91"/> <div eID="gen12138" type="x-p"/>

entries.b87bd621bb016c0129a6613eccd30119edd4513d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6569"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 91</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.91.1-Ps.91.16">Psa 91:1-16</reference>. David is the most probable author; and the pestilence, mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13-2Sam.24.15">2Sa 24:13-15</reference>, the most probable of any special occasion to which the Psalm may refer. The changes of person allowable in poetry are here frequently made.</title> <div sID="gen10068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6569"/><hi type="bold">1. dwelleth in the secret place--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">31:20</reference>) denotes nearness to God. Such as do so abide or lodge secure from assaults, and can well use the terms of trust in <reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference>. <div eID="gen10068" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2c26fe71ea9e3349b7cb8a9e40516d6f4bb670a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6570"/><div sID="gen10069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6570"/><hi type="bold">3. snares ... [and] ... noisome pestilence--</hi>literally, "plagues of mischiefs" (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">52:7</reference>), are expressive figures for various evils. <div eID="gen10069" type="x-p"/>
entries.92b4057f79a9e13d5ff724dfd976b3f09fea12a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6571"/><div sID="gen10070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6571"/>4. For the first figure compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">De 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>.<div eID="gen10070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buckler--</hi>literally, "surrounding"--that is, a kind of shield covering all over. <div eID="gen10071" type="x-p"/>
entries.227f53c38b566de2ec32be48fcea2a25c0606eb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6572"/><div sID="gen10072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6572"/><hi type="bold">5. terror--</hi>or, what causes it (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">Pr 20:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by night--</hi>then aggravated.<div eID="gen10073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arrow--</hi>that is, of enemies. <div eID="gen10074" type="x-p"/>
entries.9255ac47ef2892cfd6a5f0041b88bbda6f55b050: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6573"/><div sID="gen10075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6573"/>7-8. The security is more valuable, as being special, and, therefore, evidently of God; and while ten thousands of the wicked fall, the righteous are in such safety that they only see the calamity. <div eID="gen10075" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b91d9190fbbc8c41a3364b190f4d52f998ef0e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6574"/><div sID="gen10076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6574"/>9-12. This exemption from evil is the result of trust in God, who employs angels as ministering spirits (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">He 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen10076" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffd8fb693032018511ca26294ae5c6a38fc5d4ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6575"/><div sID="gen10077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6575"/>13. Even the fiercest, strongest, and most insidious animals may be trampled on with impunity. <div eID="gen10077" type="x-p"/>
entries.566e810a0314776f6d1ee4b887a996af62495770: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6576"/><div sID="gen10078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6576"/>14-16. God Himself speaks (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Psa 46:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.2">75:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">3</reference>). All the terms to express safety and peace indicate the most undoubting confidence (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.5">22:5</reference>).<div eID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set his love--</hi>that of the most ardent kind. <div eID="gen10079" type="x-p"/>

entries.9bfcc3d8cb65daae88fe767cc4e65ff491a45e1c: <div eID="gen21624" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21627" type="x-p"/> The safety of the godly man, and his confidence, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference>. How he is defended and preserved, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.3-Psa.91.10">Psa 91:3-10</reference>. The angels of God are his servants, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.11">Psa 91:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.12">Psa 91:12</reference>; and he shall tread on the necks of his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.13">Psa 91:13</reference>. What God says of, and promises to, such a person, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.14-Psa.91.16">Psa 91:14-16</reference>. <div eID="gen21627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21628" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title in the Hebrew; nor can it be determined on what occasion or by whom it was composed. It is most likely by the author of the preceding; and is written as a part of it, by fifteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., commencing before the repetition of the four last words of the ninetieth. It is allowed to be one of the finest Psalms in the whole collection. Of it Simon de Muis has said: "It is one of the most excellent works of this kind which has ever appeared. It is impossible to imagine any thing more solid, more beautiful, more profound, or more ornamented. Could the Latin or any modern languages express thoroughly all the beauties and elegancies as well of the words as of the sentences, it would not be difficult to persuade the reader that we have no poem, either in Greek or Latin, comparable to this Hebrew ode." <div eID="gen21628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21630" type="x-p"/> He that dwelleth in the secret place - The Targum intimates that this is a dialogue between David, Solomon, and Jehovah. Suppose we admit this, - then <div eID="gen21630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> David asserts: "He who dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty," <reference osisRef="Psa.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference>. <div eID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> Solomon answers: "I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in him will I trust," <reference osisRef="Psa.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference>. <div eID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21633" type="x-p"/> David replies, and tells him what blessings he shall receive from God if he abide faithful, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.3-Psa.91.13">Psa 91:3-13</reference>. <div eID="gen21633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21634" type="x-p"/> Then the Supreme Being is introduced, and confirms all that David had spoken concerning Solomon, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.14-Psa.91.16">Psa 91:14-16</reference> : and thus this sacred and instructive dialogue ends. <div eID="gen21634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21635" type="x-p"/> In the secret place of the Most High - Spoken probably in reference to the Holy of holies. He who enters legitimately there shall be covered with the cloud of God's glory - the protection of the all-sufflcient God. This was the privilege of the high priest only, under the law: but under the new covenant all believers in Christ have boldness to enter tnto the holiest by the blood of Jesus; and those who thus enter are safe from every evil.
entries.63891f16ebcc080de2298d8919efdf540dc3658f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21636" type="x-p"/> I will say of the Lord - This is my experience: "He is my fortress, and in him will I continually trust."
entries.76c05c5e45b510eb1261b15ad2907d547ff77805: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21637" type="x-p"/> Surely he shall deliver thee - If thou wilt act thus, then the God in whom thou trustest will deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, from all the devices of Satan, and from all dangerous maladies. As the original word, דבר dabar, signifies a word spoken, and deber, the same letters, signifies pestilence; so some translate one way, and some another: he shall deliver thee from the evil and slanderous word; he shall deliver thee from the noisome pestilence - all blasting and injurious winds, effluvia, etc.
entries.2f69b7a0fc4ffc0355fc79e38d90ee15b8d7268c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21638" type="x-p"/> He shall cover thee with his feathers - He shall act towards thee as the hen does to her brood, - take thee under his wings when birds of prey appear, and also shelter thee from chilling blasts. This is a frequent metaphor in the sacred writings; see <reference osisRef="Psa.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.57.1">Psa 57:1</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.61.4">Psa 61:4</reference> (note), and the notes on them. The Septuagint has Εν τοις μεταφρενοις αυτου επισκιασει σοι· He will overshadow thee between his shoulders; alluding to the custom of parents carrying their weak or sick children on their backs, and having them covered even there with a mantle. Thus the Lord is represented carrying the Israelites in the wilderness. See <reference osisRef="Deu.32.11-Deu.32.12">Deu 32:11-12</reference> (note), where the metaphor is taken from the eagle. <div eID="gen21638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21639" type="x-p"/> His truth shall be thy shield and buckler - His revelation; his Bible. That truth contains promises for all times and circumstances; and these will be invariably fulfilled to him that trusts in the Lord. The fulfillment of a promise relative to defense and support is to the soul what the best shield is to the body.
entries.fc10eb5c99e820c5cc85b0d1106cdaadafb78531: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21640" type="x-p"/> The terror by night - Night is a time of terrors, because it is a time of treasons, plunder, robbery, and murder. The godly man lies down in peace, and sleeps quietly, for he trusts his body, soul, and substance, in the hand of God; and he knows that he who keepeth Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. It may also mean all spiritual foes, - the rulers of the darkness of this world. I have heard the following petition in an evening family prayer: "Blessed Lord, take us into thy protection this night; and preserve us from disease, from sudden death, from the violence of fire, from the edge of the sword, from the designs of wicked men, and from the influence of malicious spirits!" <div eID="gen21640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21641" type="x-p"/> Nor for the arrow - The Chaldee translates this verse, "Thou shalt not fear the demons that walk by night; nor the arrow of the angel of death which is shot in the day time." Thou needest not to fear a sudden and unprovided-for death.
entries.47fc5c41c7581fd21d5e292e8b6d6cbb655647c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21642" type="x-p"/> Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday - The rabbins supposed that the empire of death was under two demons, one of which ruled by day, the other by night. The Vulgate and Septuagint have - the noonday devil. The ancients thought that there were some demons who had the power to injure particularly at noonday. To this Theocritus refers, Id. 1: ver. 15: - Ου θεμις, ω ποιμαν, το μεσαμβρινον, ου θεμις αμμιν Συρισδεν· τον Πανα δεδοικαμες· η γαρ απ' αγρας Τανικα κεκμακως αμπαυεται, εντι γε πικρος, Και οἱ αει δριμεια χολα ποτι ῥινι καθηται. "It is not lawful, it is not lawful, O shepherd, to play on the flute at noonday: we fear Pan, who at that hour goes to sleep in order to rest himself after the fatigues of the chase; then he is dangerous, and his wrath easily kindled." <div eID="gen21642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21643" type="x-p"/> Lucan, in the horrible account he gives us of a grove sacred to some barbarous power, worshipped with the most horrid rites, refers to the same superstition: - <div eID="gen21643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21644" type="x-p"/> Lucus erat longo nunquam violatus ab aevo, <div eID="gen21644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21645" type="x-p"/> Non illum cultu populi propiore frequentant, <div eID="gen21645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21646" type="x-p"/> Sed cessere deis: medio cum Phoebus in axe est. <div eID="gen21646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21647" type="x-p"/> Aut coelum nox atra tenet, pavet ipse sacerdos <div eID="gen21647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21648" type="x-p"/> Accessus, dominumque timet deprendere luci. <div eID="gen21648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21649" type="x-p"/> Lucan, lib. iii., ver. 399. "Not far away, for ages past, had stood <div eID="gen21649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21650" type="x-p"/> An old inviolated sacred wood: <div eID="gen21650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21651" type="x-p"/> The pious worshippers approach not near, <div eID="gen21651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21652" type="x-p"/> But shun their gods, and kneel with distant fear: <div eID="gen21652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21653" type="x-p"/> The priest himself, when, or the day or night <div eID="gen21653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21654" type="x-p"/> Rolling have reached their full meridian height, <div eID="gen21654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21655" type="x-p"/> Refrains the gloomy paths with wary feet, <div eID="gen21655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21656" type="x-p"/> Dreading the demon of the grove to meet; <div eID="gen21656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21657" type="x-p"/> Who, terrible to sight, at that fixed hour <div eID="gen21657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21658" type="x-p"/> Still treads the round about this dreary bower." <div eID="gen21658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21659" type="x-p"/> Rowe. <div eID="gen21659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21660" type="x-p"/> It has been stated among the heathens that the gods should be worshipped at all times, but the demons should be worshipped at midday: probably because these demons, having been employed during the night, required rest at noonday and that was the most proper time to appease them. See Calmet on this place. Both the Vulgate and Septuagint seem to have reference to this superstition. <div eID="gen21660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21661" type="x-p"/> The Syriac understands the passage of a pestilential wind, that blows at noonday. Aquila translates, of the bite of the noonday demon.
entries.5407950f4c371f91b6b2fd8d4d4ae1575a585fc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> A thousand shall fall at thy side - Calmet thinks this place should be translated thus: "A thousand enemies may fall upon thee on one side, and ten thousand may fall upon thee on thy right hand: but they shall not come nigh thee to take away thy life." It is a promise of perfect protection, and the utmost safety.
entries.df36a87e73835bdfa8dac2b00d66f3765e2f1ca3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21663" type="x-p"/> The reward of the wicked - Thou shalt not only be safe thyself, but thou shalt see all thy enemies discomfited and cast down.
entries.fd30fcf5ae989480f49e3cde740f8b131cc1c9f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21664" type="x-p"/> Because thou hast made the Lord - Seeing thou hast taken Jehovah, the Most High, for thy portion and thy refuge, no evil shall come nigh thy dwelling; thou shalt be safe in thy soul, body, household, and property, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.10">Psa 91:10</reference>. Every pious man may expect such protection from his God and Father.
entries.19d7165cfb27dcc9c3a04963856bd6375ba2ac97: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21665" type="x-p"/> He shall give his angels charge over thee - Evil spirits may attempt to injure thee; but they shall not be able. The angels of God shall have an especial charge to accompany, defend, and preserve thee; and against their power, the influence of evil spirits cannot prevail. These will, when necessary, turn thy steps out of the wag of danger; ward it off when it comes in thy ordinary path; suggest to thy mind prudent counsels, profitable designs, and pious purposes; and thus minister to thee as a child of God, and an heir of salvation. <div eID="gen21665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21666" type="x-p"/> To keep thee in all thy ways - The path of duty is the way of safety. <div eID="gen21666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21667" type="x-p"/> Thou canst not reasonably expect protection if thou walk not in the way of obedience. Thy ways are the paths of duty, which God's word and providence have marked out for thee. The way of sin is not thy way - thy duty, thy interest. Keep in thy own ways, not in those of sin, Satan, the world, and the flesh; and God will take care of thee.
entries.0e31ab1aa3d6a61f8dae1fcc9a077c69d65ed8d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21668" type="x-p"/> They shall bear thee up in their hands - Take the same care of thee as a nurse does of a weak and tender child; lead thee, - teach thee to walk, - lift thee up out of the way of danger, "lest thou shouldst dash thy foot against a stone," receive any kind of injury, or be prevented from pursuing thy path with safety and comfort. <div eID="gen21668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21669" type="x-p"/> Let us remember that it is God, whose these angels are; He gives them charge from Him they receive their commission, - to Him they are responsible for their charge. From God thou art to expect them; and for their help he alone is to receive the praise. It is expressly said, He shall give his angels charge; to show that they are not to be prayed to nor praised but God alone, whose servants they are. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.4.6">Mat 4:6</reference>.
entries.d349a7edf32c5d122150689705bf9ebb375196f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21670" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder - Even the king of the forest shall not be able to injure thee; should one of these attack thee, the angels whom God sends will give thee an easy victory over him. And even the asp, (פתן pethen), one of the most venomous of serpents, shall not be able to injure thee. <div eID="gen21670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21671" type="x-p"/> The asp is a very small serpent, and peculiar to Egypt and Libya. Its poison kills without the possibility of a remedy. Those who are bitten by it die in about from three to eight hours; and it is said they die by sleep, without any kind of pain. Lord Bacon says the asp is less painful than all the other instruments of death. He supposes it to have an affinity to opium, but to be less disagreeable in its operation. It was probably an this account that Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, chose to die by the asp, as she was determined to prevent the designs of Augustus, who intended to have carried her captive to Rome to grace his triumph. <div eID="gen21671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21672" type="x-p"/> The dragon shalt thou trample - The תנין tannin, which we translate dragon, means often any large aquatic animal; and perhaps here the crocodile or alligator.
entries.b701f59aa75db1cecb7ef3b7f8b98dcc54a08254: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21673" type="x-p"/> Because he hath set his love upon me - Here the Most High is introduced as confirming the word of his servant. He has fixed his love - his heart and soul, on me. <div eID="gen21673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21674" type="x-p"/> Therefore will I deliver him - I will save him in all troubles, temptations, and evils of every kind. <div eID="gen21674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21675" type="x-p"/> I will set him on high - I will place him out of the reach of all his enemies. I will honor and ennoble him, because he hath known my name - because he has loved, honored, and served me, and rendered me that worship which is my due. He has known me to be the God of infinite mercy and love.
entries.36433cc046ef172a2a4876555d00a9b598e75b65: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21676" type="x-p"/> He shall call upon me - He must continue to pray; all his blessings must come in this way, when he calls, I will answer him - I will give him whatever is best for him. <div eID="gen21676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21677" type="x-p"/> I will be with him in trouble - Literally, I am with him. עמו אנכי immo anochi; as soon as the trouble comes, I are there. <div eID="gen21677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21678" type="x-p"/> I will deliver him - For his good I may permit him to be exercised for a time, but delivered he shall be. <div eID="gen21678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21679" type="x-p"/> And honor him - אכבדהו acabbedehu, "I will glorify him." I will load him with honor; that honor that comes from God. I will even show to men how highly I prize such.
entries.282c0557468b917b4c8e26fb926578268381ad08: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21680" type="x-p"/> With long life - Literally, With length of days will I fill him up. <div eID="gen21680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21681" type="x-p"/> He shall neither live a useless life, nor die before his time. He shall live happy and die happy. <div eID="gen21681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21682" type="x-p"/> And show him my salvation - ואראהו בשועתי vearehu bishuathi, "I will make him see (or contemplate) in my salvation." He shall discover infinite lengths, breadths, depths, and heights, in my salvation. He shall feel boundless desires, and shall discover that I have provided boundless gratifications for them. He shall dwell in my glory, and throughout eternity increase in his resemblance to and enjoyment of me. Thus shall it be done to the man whom the Lord delighteth to honor; and he delights to honor that man who places his love on him. In a word, he shall have a long life in this world, and an eternity of blessedness in the world to come.  <chapter eID="Ps.91"/> <div eID="gen21682" type="x-p"/>

entries.2c1c8dd07a84a694ae3508d9b0b8ad054f967c91: <div eID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Talismanic Song in Time of War and Pestilence</title> <div sID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> The primeval song is followed by an anonymous song (inscribed by the lxx without any warrant τῷ Δαυίδ), the time of whose composition cannot be determined; and it is only placed in this order because the last verse accords with the last verse but one of Ps 90. There the revelation of Jahve’s work is prayed for, and here Jahve promises: <hi type="italic">I will grant him to see My salvation</hi>; the “work of Jahve” is His realized “salvation.” The two Psalms also have other points of contact, e.g., in the מעון referred to God (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 60). <div eID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> In this Psalm, the Invocavit Psalm of the church, which praises the protecting and rescuing grace which he who believingly takes refuge in God experiences in all times of danger and distress,<note placement="foot">Hence in J. <hi type="italic">Shabbath</hi> 8, col. 2, and <hi type="italic">Midrash</hi> <hi type="italic">Shocher</hi> <hi type="italic">tob</hi> on <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> and elsewhere, it is called, together with <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8">Psa 3:1-8</reference>, (פגעים) שיר פגועין, a song of occurrences, i.e., a protective (or talismanic) song in times of dangers that may befall one, just as Sebald Heyden’s Psalm-song, “He who is in the protection of the Most High and resigns himself to God,” is inscribed “Preservative against the pestilence.”</note> the relation of <reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> meets us at the very beginning as a perplexing riddle. If we take <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> as a clause complete in itself, then it is tautological. If we take אמר in <reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference> as a participle (Jerome, <hi type="italic">dicens</hi>) instead of אמר, ending with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> because a construct from (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">Psa 136:6</reference>), then the participial subject would have a participial predicate: “He who sitteth is saying,” which is inelegant and also improbable, since אמר in other instances is always the <hi type="italic">1st pers. fut</hi>. If we take אמר as <hi type="italic">1st pers. fut</hi>. and <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> as an apposition of the subject expressed in advance: as such an one who sitteth.... I say, then we stumble against יתלונן; this transition of the participle to the finite verb, especially without the copula (וּבצל), is confusing. If, however, we go on and read further into the Psalm, we find that the same difficulty as to the change of person recurs several times later on, just as in the opening. Olshausen, Hupfeld, and Hitzig get rid of this difficulty by all sorts of conjectures. But a reason for this abrupt change of the person is that dramatic arrangement recognised even in the Targum, although awkwardly indicated, which, however, as first of all clearly discerned by J. D. Michaelis and Maurer. There are, to wit, two voices that speak (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:1-8</reference>), and at last the voice of Jahve comes in as a third. His closing utterance, rich in promise, forms, perhaps not unaccidentally, a seven-line strophe. Whether the Psalm came also to be executed in liturgical use thus with several voices, perhaps by three choirs, we cannot tell; but the poet certainly laid it out dramatically, as the translation represents it. In spite of the many echoes of earlier models, it is one of the freshest and most beautiful Psalms, resembling the second part of Isaiah in its light-winged, richly coloured, and transparent diction.
entries.5e19394c7790c24b0add465d04be062e92ac7538: <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1-Ps.91.2">Psa 91:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> As the concealing One, God is called עליון, the inaccessibly high One; and as the shadowing One שׁדּי, the invincibly almighty One. Faith, however, calls Him by His covenant name (<hi type="italic">Heilsname</hi>) יהוה and, with the suffix of appropriation, אלהי (<hi type="italic">my</hi> God). In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> we are reminded of the expressions of the Book of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.39.28">Job 39:28</reference>, concerning the eagle’s building its nest in its eyrie. According to the accentuation, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference></hi> ought to be rendered with Geier, “<hi type="italic">Dicit: in Domino meo (or Domini) latibulum</hi>, etc.” But the combination אמר לה is more natural, since the language of address follows in both halves of the verse.
entries.432397049fb933913ee496730ad5ac039ae9964a: <reference osisRef="Ps.91.3-Ps.91.9">Psa 91:3-9</reference> יקושׁ, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.5">Pro 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.26">Jer 5:26</reference>, is the dullest toned from for יקושׁ or יוקשׁ, Psa 124:7. What is meant is death, or “he who has the power of death,” <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb 2:14</reference>, cf. 2Ti 2:26. “The snare of the fowler” is a figure for the peril of one’s life, Ecc 9:12. In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference> we have to call to mind <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference> : God protects His own as an eagle with its large strong wing. אברה is <hi type="italic">nom. unitatis</hi>, a pinion, to אבר, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>; and the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הסך, from סכך, with the dative of the object, like the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference>, signifies to afford covering, protection. The ἅπαξ λεγ. סחרה, according to its stem-word, is that which encompasses anything round about, and here beside צנּה, a weapon of defence surrounding the body on all sides; therefore not corresponding to the Syriac <hi type="italic">sḥārtā'</hi>, a stronghold (סהר, מסגּרת), but to Syriac <hi type="italic">sabrā'</hi>, a shield. The Targum translates צנּה with תּריסא, θυρεός, and סחרה with עגילא, which points to the round <hi type="italic">parma</hi>. אמתּו is the truth of the divine promises. This is an impregnable defence (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) in war-times, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.5">Psa 91:5</reference>, against nightly surprises, and in the battle by day; (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) in times of pestilence, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">Psa 91:6</reference>, when the destroying angel, who passes through and destroys the people (<reference osisRef="Exod.11.4">Exo 11:4</reference>), can do no harm to him who has taken refuge in God, either in the midnight or the noontide hours. The future יהלך is a more rhythmical and, in the signification to rage (as of disease) and to vanish away, a more usual form instead of ילך. The lxx, Aquila, and Symmachus erroneously associate the demon name שׁד with ישׁוּד. It is a metaplastic (as if formed from שׁוּד morf de) future for ישׁד, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">Pro 29:6</reference>, ירוּן, and <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa 42:4</reference>, ירוּץ, <hi type="italic">frangetur</hi>. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.91.7">Psa 91:7</reference></hi> a hypothetical protasis: <hi type="italic">si cadant</hi>; the preterite would signify <hi type="italic">cediderint</hi>, Ew. §357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. With רק that which will solely and exclusively take place is introduced. Burk correctly renders: <hi type="italic">nullam cum peste rem habebis, nisi ut videas</hi>. Only a spectator shalt thou be, and that with thine own eyes, being they self inaccessible and left to survive, conscious that thou thyself art a living one in contrast with those who are dying. And thou shalt behold, like Israel on the night of the Passover, the just retribution to which the evil-doers fall a prey. שׁלּמה, recompense, retribution, is a hapaxlegomenon, cf. שׁלּמים, Isa 34:8. Ascribing the glory to God, the second voice confirms or ratifies these promises.

PSALM 91
In this psalm we are taught that God watches over the safety of his people, and never fails them in the hour of danger. They are exhorted to advance through all perils, secure in the confidence of his protection. The truth inculcated is one of great use, for though many talk much of God’s providence, and profess to believe that he exercises a special guardianship over his own children, few are found actually willing to intrust their safety to him.
“Early, after the dark night of afflictions.” — Ainsworth.
Psalm 91:1-4
1. He that dwelleth in the secret place of the High One shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. 2. I will say to Jehovah, He is my hope and my fortress: my God; in him will I hope. 3. Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, from the noxious pestilence. 4. He shall protect thee with his wings, and under his feathers shalt thou be safe; his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
 
1 He that dwelleth in the secret place of the High One. Some Hebrew interpreters read the three first verses as one continuous sentence, down to the words, he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler The whole would then run thus — “He who dwells in the covert of the Most High, and abides under his shadow, to him will I say of Jehovah, that he is his hope and defense, and the God in whom he may safely rest, for he shall deliver him from the snare,” etc. This is evidently a forced construction to put upon the verses, and the reason which has led some to adopt it is weak and insufficient. They consider that the first verse repeats the same thing twice, and therefore conveys no proper meaning. But this is a great mistake; for the inspired penman of the psalm, whoever he may have been, states two ideas quite distinct, That he who is hid under the Divine protection occupies a safe and secure position, where no hostile weapon can reach him. Or should the verse be read — He who has God to be the guardian of his safety shall rest under the shadow of God; still the second clause would retain an emphatic meaning, for the power of God would be contrasted with that weak defense which man is able to extend. Those, too, who dwell in the secret place of God are here said by the Psalmist to dwell under his shadow, in the sense that they experience to what a rich extent his protection reaches. Men generally seek out a great-variety of hiding-places, having recourse to one or another, according as the calamities are different which threaten to overtake them; but here we are taught that the only safe and impregnable fortress to which we can betake ourselves is the protection of God. He contrasts the security of those who trust in God with the vanity of all other confidences by which we are apt to delude ourselves.
